question: to the Commission Jorge Buxadé Villalba (PfE) Subject:

Between 2019 and 2024, the EU issued more than 13 000 new regulations. In the financial sector, EU regulatory output has grown by more than 700 % in three decades, reaching around 1 629 documents – some 95 500 pages – across the banking and capital markets regulatory framework. More than 60 % of European companies identify regulation as an obstacle to investment, and 55 % of SMEs point to the regulatory and administrative burden as their biggest challenge. In the European Round Table for Industry survey for the second half of 2025, only 8 % of the CEOs consulted planned to increase investment in Europe, while 45 % expected to invest more than expected in the US. Does the Commission: 1.
understand that the complexity and quantity of its regulation – especially in the energy, financial, food and transport sectors – is creating regulatory chaos and discouraging investments?
agree that European companies are increasingly dedicating resources to compliance and reporting rather than investing in technology, employment or innovation?
consider itself responsible for the gradual loss of competitiveness, industrial capacity and quality of life in Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.8.2026) Regulatory complexity can affect competitiveness. This is why the Commission is pursuing modernisation and simplification of European legislation and is effectively reducing the administrative burdens for companies. The Commission has a target to lower the administrative burden by at least 25% and at least 35% for small and medium-sized enterprises. To this end, it has so far proposed 12 omnibus packages and other simplification proposals, with net recurrent cost savings of some EUR 18 billion. Half of the proposals for the Commission work programme 2026 are simplification proposals. Looking ahead, the recent Communication ‘A Simpler, Clearer and Better Enforced EU Rulebook’1 contains a Regulatory Deep Cleaning Action Plan with 12 policy areas, including the energy, financial, food and transport sectors mentioned in the question. It will tackle inconsistencies, outdated, overlapping or redundant provisions, or overly complex rules that hinder competitiveness and innovation. The Communication also includes simplicity by design as a new way of making legislation. The Commission is acting decisively and swiftly to address EU loss of competitiveness. It is a shared responsibility with co-legislators to make this ambition a concrete deliverable.
